titre: Eastern Greenland (1933): A Minister's Answer That Binds a State
accroche: On July 22, 1919, a Norwegian minister says he will not make difficulties. On April 5, 1933, the Hague Court rules that this sentence binds Norway.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 10, 1931, a Norwegian royal proclamation declares a territory on the east coast of Greenland, between Carlsberg Fjord to the south and Bessel Fjord to the north, from 71°30' to 75°40' north latitude, taken and placed under Norwegian sovereignty. Denmark, which considers itself sovereign over the whole island, brings the matter before the Permanent Court of International Justice two days later, on July 12.

## A sentence in a record of conversation

To establish its rights, Denmark invokes, among other arguments, a conversation in 1919. In Paris, a four-member commission is to examine the question of Spitsbergen, over which Norway hopes to obtain sovereignty. On July 14, 1919, the Danish minister in Christiania tells the Norwegian Minister for Foreign Affairs, Nils Claus Ihlen, that his country will not oppose Norway's wishes regarding Spitsbergen, and that it expects Norway not to make difficulties over Greenland. Ihlen replies that the question will be examined. On July 22, he records in his own minute: he informed the Danish minister that the Norwegian government would not make difficulties in settling this question. He dates it and initials it.

The Court begins by rejecting Denmark's reading. These words do not amount to recognition of an already existing sovereignty: the wording is in the future tense, and two years later Denmark was still asking Norway for the recognition it wanted. But the Court sees in them a commitment. It holds it beyond all dispute that a reply of this nature, given by the Minister for Foreign Affairs on behalf of his government, in response to a request by the diplomatic representative of a foreign power, on a question within his competence, is binding upon the country to which the minister belongs. Norway objects that Denmark had not announced in 1919 its plan for an exclusion regime over all of Greenland, decreed on May 10, 1921. The Court answers that Norway could have foreseen it. The promise was unconditional and definitive: Norway must refrain from contesting Danish sovereignty over the whole of Greenland, and a fortiori from occupying a part of it.

## The shift

The operative part, adopted by twelve votes to two (Judge Anzilotti and Judge ad hoc Vogt dissent), declares the occupation of July 10, 1931 unlawful and invalid. To think that Ihlen's sentence gave Greenland to Denmark would be a mistake. The Court says something else. It first examines the Danish title itself, based on the continuous exercise of State authority, and holds that on the critical date of July 10, 1931, Denmark possessed a valid title to the whole island. It adds that this finding alone is enough to make the occupation unlawful and invalid. It observes that tribunals are satisfied with very little in the way of actual exercise of sovereignty when no other State can claim a superior title, especially in thinly populated or uninhabited regions. Only afterward does it examine Denmark's second argument, the commitments made by Norway, and it retains three: the commitment not to contest Danish sovereignty, made at the end of the Dano-Norwegian union (1814-1819); the agreements in which Norway accepted that Greenland was Danish or left it outside their scope; and Ihlen's declaration.

The third of these commitments rests on very little: no treaty, no plenipotentiary, just a sentence said to a diplomat and noted in a single line by its author, dated 22/7 - 19 and initialed Ih.

repere.texte: On April 5, 1933, the Permanent Court of International Justice rules, by twelve votes to two, that the Norwegian occupation of July 10, 1931 is unlawful and invalid: Denmark had a valid title to all of Greenland, and Norway was bound by the Ihlen declaration of July 22, 1919.
repere.source: Permanent Court of International Justice, Legal Status of Eastern Greenland, Series A/B No. 53, judgment of April 5, 1933

carte.punch: A sentence said to a diplomat in 1919 bound Norway before the Hague Court in 1933.
carte.idee: In 1933, the Court finds the 1931 Norwegian occupation invalid: Denmark had title to the entire island, and Norway had committed itself in 1919 through the oral reply of its minister Ihlen, which binds the country.

quiz.question: Why does the Court find that Minister Ihlen's reply binds Norway?
choix: Because it recognized Danish sovereignty, already existing, over all of Greenland, without condition
Because Norway had confirmed it in writing in an official note to Denmark in 1921
Because Denmark had threatened to oppose Norwegian sovereignty over Spitsbergen in Paris
Because a foreign minister's reply, on behalf of the government, binds his country
quiz.explication: The Court rejects the idea of a definitive recognition: the wording is in the future tense and Denmark asked for recognition again two years later. Norway even refused in 1921 to confirm it in writing. Denmark did not threaten over Spitsbergen; it said it would not oppose Norway's wishes. The commitment comes from the author's position and the form of the exchange.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What territory does the Norwegian royal proclamation of July 10, 1931 cover?
choix: The whole island of Greenland, including its west coast
A territory on the east coast of Greenland, between Carlsberg and Bessel fjords
Spitsbergen, which Norway had claimed since 1919
An exclusion zone decreed at the same time over all of Greenland
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The July 10, 1931 proclamation covers the east coast of Greenland, between Carlsberg Fjord to the south and Bessel Fjord to the north, not the whole island.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what does the Court first base its decision, even before examining the Norwegian commitments?
choix: A unanimous vote of the judges in favor of Denmark
A Norwegian commitment made at the end of the Dano-Norwegian union
The Danish title, based on the continuous exercise of State authority
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court first examines the Danish title based on the continuous exercise of State authority, and holds that this finding alone is enough to invalidate the occupation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many judges voted for the operative part of the April 5, 1933 judgment, and how many against?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The operative part is adopted by twelve votes to two, with Judges Anzilotti and Vogt not following the majority.
